game.name: Downwell
game.short_description: Downwell is a curious game about a young person venturing down a well in search of untold treasures with only his Gunboots to protect him.

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm gonna put it as a high D tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 1 (2023)
commentary.summary: Downwell is a minimalist roguelike where you fall down a deep well instead of climbing, using only left, right and jump, with the jump button also firing your gun downward. He thinks it is amazingly well designed and feels like a game-jam idea turned into a fun game. It is punishing and purely skill-based, and it becomes repetitive because there are no distinct builds. He finished it once and does not plan to return, so he places it high in D tier, explicitly not counting its low price.
praise: Very minimalistic yet amazingly well designed
Unique gimmick of descending as fast as possible rather than advancing forward
Simple controls: left, right, jump, with jump again shooting downward
Different weapons and upgrades found across runs
Skill-based: progress comes from mastering the mechanics, never from feeling overpowered
Feels like a quick game-jam idea turned into a really fun game
criticism: Gets very repetitive since there are no unique builds
Progress is only about how far down you can go
Very punishing: you have little health and take damage easily
The well is quite deep; he finished it once and had no desire to return
unique_points: Inverts the usual direction of games by making the goal going down as fast as possible
Single-button-combo design where jumping and shooting share an input
Pure skill-based roguelike with no power fantasy
commentary.quote: it's actually really amazingly well designed
design_criteria: Personal entertainment: rated on how much he enjoyed playing it, not on price
Build diversity: lacks unique builds, making it repetitive
Skill vs power: purely skill-based with no overpowered moments
Replayability: he felt done after one completion

community.one_liner: A one-man-made (Moppin) vertical arcade roguelite where you fall down a procedurally generated well, using gunboots as both jump and weapon, in a stark black/white/red pixel style.
community.consensus_summary: Downwell is received as a small arcade classic: Steam sits at Overwhelmingly Positive (about 96.5% of roughly 8,600 reviews), OpenCritic at 83 (84% of critics recommend) and Metacritic PC at 81, with stronger scores on iOS (91) and Switch (88). Critics and players praise the tight, instantly readable controls, the one-more-run loop and the style/module variety. Complaints cluster around high difficulty and run-to-run luck, thin long-term progression and power-up pool, and a few missing quality-of-life options on PC. Metacritic user score is notably lower (6.8, Mixed) than Steam, suggesting a split between fans and people who bounce off the speed. It is a finished, cheap game (about $2.99 on Steam) that has been ported widely (iOS, PC, Android, PS4/Vita, Switch, PS5) rather than an early-access or abandoned title.
best_things: Extremely responsive, simple controls: left/right plus one button that both jumps and fires the gunboots, so movement and combat are the same verb
Addictive short runs that invite 'just one more try'; good for quick sessions and works in a vertical display mode on Switch
Distinctive, minimalist look (black, white and red with swappable palettes) and a strong soundtrack, including the music cutting in the moment you land
Deceptively deep mechanics: combos, gem collection, ammo management and stomping enemies reward skilled play
Styles, modules and perks that change how a run plays, giving variety within a very small game
Bargain price and heavy replay value; many Steam reviewers report owning it on several platforms and playing for over 100 hours
Hard mode and a meaningful final boss give a reason to keep going for players who master it
Polished feel for a solo-developed debut; awards included Destructoid Best Mobile Game of 2015 and GDC Best Debut nominations
Plays well as a low-commitment pick-up game: several Steam reviewers play it while waiting in queues or alongside podcasts, and some own it on multiple platforms
worst_things: Very punishing: tiny health pool and fast pace mean one or two mistakes end a run, which many players find unfair or overwhelming
Runs feel luck dependent (level layout, upgrade offers, shop items), so skill cannot always rescue a bad run
Enemy density late in a run can make it hard to spot your character and produces deaths players call unavoidable
Some color palettes reduce readability, since gameplay relies on three colors and a few palettes only have two
PC port lacks basics: no proper options menu, no jump remapping on keyboard, no screen shake toggle according to negative Steam reviews
Hit detection and movement complaints from some players when the screen is busy
improvements: A full options menu on PC: key remapping (jump cannot be rebound), screen shake toggle and other accessibility settings
Stronger persistent progression or meta-unlocks so repeated runs feel cumulative (Game Informer cited lack of long-term incentive)
A larger and better balanced perk and weapon pool; reviewers note a few options are clearly stronger than the rest
Better readability in busy rooms and in alternate palettes, with gameplay-critical colors kept distinct
More difficulty options or an easier entry ramp for newcomers who find it too hard
Better support for widescreen/horizontal displays, where the vertical aspect ratio is awkward
unique_things: Gunboots: the jump doubles as the weapon and as a fall-slowing tool, fusing platforming and shooting into one input
Vertical, downward-only descent structure with short runs, closer to an arcade score-attack than a typical exploratory roguelike
Strict limited palette (black/white/red, blue for water) with many unlockable palettes that act as collectible skins
Combo-and-gem economy where stomping chains without touching ground drives both score and currency
Originally designed for mobile and vertical play, and it still plays well on phones and rotated displays
Soundtrack that kicks in on landing, tying audio directly to the core movement loop
tedious_or_disliked: Reaching proficiency can feel like grinding through many quick deaths with little carried over between runs
Repetitive runs despite procedural generation, noted by Game Informer
Random level, shop and upgrade rolls that some players feel do not reward learning from mistakes
The pace is too fast and stressful for some, who describe it as nearly unplayable without inhuman reactions
Forced screen shake and missing accessibility/control options on PC frustrate a few players
divisive_points: Difficulty: fans call it tough but fair and mastery-driven, while detractors call it luck-heavy and overwhelming (Steam 96.5% positive versus Metacritic user score 6.8)
Depth versus repetition: Eurogamer and Nintendo Life describe real depth, Game Informer and others find the run structure thin after the first hours
Minimalist presentation: praised as charming and stylish, but the limited palettes and audio bother some players
Whether the game suits PC: PC Games felt it was cut to mobile needs and felt odd with PC controls, while many Steam players love it
community.reception_notes: Launched October 2015 on iOS and Windows (Android January 2016, PS4/Vita May 2016, later Switch and PS5) to broad acclaim, winning TouchArcade Game of the Week and Destructoid Best Mobile Game of 2015 and earning Game Awards and GDC nominations. The critic scores are strongest on iOS and Switch and lowest on PS4/PC, consistent with its mobile-first design; PC Games was a notable dissenter at 70% over the PC feel. Metacritic user reviews are mixed (55% positive, 29% mixed, 16% negative on about 198 ratings) while Steam remains very high, and recent Steam negatives in 2025-26 still focus on speed, luck and missing PC options, suggesting no major control/options patch has resolved them. Steam estimates (SteamSpy 200k-500k owners; steam-revenue-calculator about $817k gross and $241k net to the developer) are rough Boxleiter-style figures across Steam only and exclude mobile and console, where the game sold widely.
